source_text: Ἑξῆς τούτοις φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι τῷ ἡγησαμένῳ σφῶν ἑπόμενοι Μωϋσεῖ αἰπόλοι καὶ ποιμένες. ἀγροίκοις ἀπάταις ψυχαγωγηθέντες ἕνα ἐνόμισαν εἶναι θεόν. δεικνύτω τοίνυν πῶς, αἰπόλων καὶ ποιμένων ἀλόγως, ὡς οἴεται, ἀποστάντων τοῦ σέβειν θεοὺς. αὐτὸς δύναται παραστῆσαι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν καθ᾿ Ἕλληνας θεῶν ἢ τοὺς λοιποὺς βαρβάρους. δεικνύτω τοίνυν ὑπόστασιν καὶ οὐσίαν Μνημοσύνης γεννώσης ἀπὸ Διὸς τὰς Μούσας. ἢ Θέμιδος τὰς Ὥρας, ἢ τὰς Χάριτας ἀεὶ γυμνὰς παραστησάτω δύνασθαι κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ὑφεστηκέναι. ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δυνήσεται τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα σωματοποιεῖσθαι δοκοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων δεικνύναι θεούς. τί γὰρ μᾶλλον οἱ Ἑλλήνων μῦθοι περὶ θεῶν ἀληθεῖς ἢ, φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν, οἱ Αἰγυπτίων, οὐκ εἰδότων τῇ σφῶν διαλέκτῳ Μνημοσύνην μητέρα Μουσῶν ἐννέα οὐδὲ Θέμιν Ὡρῶν οὐδὲ Εὐρυνόμην μίαν τῶν Χαρίτων οὐδὲ τὰ λοιπὰ ὀνόματα αὐτῶν; πόσῳ οὖν ἐνεργέστερον καὶ πάντων τούτων τῶν ἀναπλασμάτων βέλτιον τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων πειθόμενον τοῖς κατὰ τὴν εὐταξίαν τοῦ κόσμου σέβειν τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτοῦ ἑνὸς ὄντος ἕνα καὶ συμπνέοντος αὐτοῦ ὅλῳ ἑαυτῷ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μὴ δυναμένῳ ὑπὸ πολλῶν δημιουργῶν γεγονέναι, ὡς οὐδ᾿ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ψυχῶν συνέχεσθαι ὅλον τὸν οὐρανὸν κινουσῶν· ἀρκεῖ γὰρ μία ἡ φέρουσα ὅλην τὴν ἀπλανῆ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἐπὶ δυσμὰς καὶ ἐμπεριλαβοῦσα ἔνδον πάντα. ὧν χρείαν ἔχει ὁ κόσμος, τὰ μὴ αὐτοτελῆ. πάντα γὰρ μέρη κόσμου, οὐδὲν δὲ μέρος ὅλου θεός· δεῖ γὰρ εἶναι τὸν θεὸν μὴ ἀτελῆ. ὥσπερ ἐστὶ τὸ μέρος ἀτελές. τάχα δὲ βαθύτερος λόγος δείξει ὅτι κυρίως θεὸς ὥσπερ οὐκ ἔστι μέρος οὕτως οὐδὲ ὅλον, ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅλον ἐκ μερῶν ἐστι· καὶ οὐχ αἱρεῖ λόγος παραδέξασθαι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν εἶναι ἐκ μερῶν. ὧν ἕκαστον οὐ δύναται ὅπερ τὰ ἄλλα μέρη.
pass_a_gloss: Next to these things Celsus says that having followed Moses, who was their leader, they were shepherds and goatherds, and having been deceived by rustic deceptions, they thought there was one God. Let him show, then, how, irrationally, as he thinks, shepherds and goatherds, having revolted from worshiping gods. He himself is able to present the multitude of gods according to the Greeks or the other barbarians. Let him show, then, the substance and being of Mnemosyne, who generated the Muses from Zeus, or of Themis, who generated the Horae, or let him present the Charites, who are always naked, as being able to exist in being. But he will not be able to show that the Greek fabrications, which seem to be embodied from things, are gods. For what is more true, the myths of the Greeks about gods or, for example, those of the Egyptians, who do not know in their own language Mnemosyne as the mother of the nine Muses, nor Themis as the mother of the Horae, nor Eurynome as one of the Charites, nor the rest of their names? How much more, then, is it more effective and better than all these fabrications to be persuaded by the things that are seen to worship the creator of the world, who is one and the same, and who breathes together with the whole world, and because of this is not able to have been made by many creators, just as the whole heaven is not held together by many souls moving it; for one soul is enough, which carries the whole heaven from east to west and encompasses all things inside, which the world needs, the things that are not self-sufficient. For all parts of the world are not self-sufficient, and no part is the whole God; for God must be not incomplete. Just as a part is incomplete. Perhaps a deeper argument will show that God is not, properly speaking, a part, just as he is not a whole, since the whole is from parts; and reason does not accept that the God over all things is from parts, each of which is not able to do what the other parts do.

choices.why: indicating the reason for their actions
comparing the effectiveness of different beliefs

pass_b_english: Celsus goes on to claim that those who followed Moses as their leader were merely shepherds and goatherds, deceived by rustic tricks into believing there is only one God. He ought to demonstrate how, in his view, such herdsmen could irrationally abandon the worship of the many gods. He himself claims to be able to set forth the whole crowd of Greek deities or those of other peoples, so let him produce the very substance and reality of Mnemosyne giving birth to the Muses from Zeus, or of Themis bearing the Hours, or of the ever-naked Graces existing as genuine beings. He will not succeed, for the Greek inventions that appear to be embodied from natural phenomena cannot be shown to be true gods. After all, why should Greek myths about the gods be considered truer than, say, those of the Egyptians, who in their own language know nothing of Mnemosyne as mother of the nine Muses, or of Themis as mother of the Hours, or of Eurynome as one of the Graces, or of the rest of their names? How much more effective and superior to all such fabrications is it to be persuaded by the visible order of the world to worship its Creator, who is one and the same, who breathes together with the whole cosmos, and who therefore could not have been fashioned by many creators, just as the entire heaven is not held together by many souls moving it. One soul suffices to carry the whole fixed heaven from east to west and to encompass within itself all that the world requires, all that is not self-sufficient. For every part of the world is dependent, and no part is the whole God, since God must not be incomplete, as a part is. Indeed, a deeper line of reasoning may show that, properly speaking, God is neither a part nor a whole, because a whole is composed of parts, and reason refuses to accept that the God over all could be constituted from parts, each of which cannot do what the others do.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex philosophical arguments regarding the unity of God and the composition of the cosmos. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek text. The distinction between 'part' and 'whole' in the final sentences is preserved correctly.
